correctness.rationale: Only prime support matters. An odd prime with a root of −1 is 1 mod 4, so except for 5 it exceeds 7. For two hits at displacement d=1,…,7, subtraction gives 2(a+i)≡−d, hence p divides d²+4; factoring 5,8,13,20,29,40,53 leaves only separations 3,5,7 for p≠2,5. Such a prime hits at most one slot of a fixed parity and at most two slots in the whole block (p>7, and at most two roots). With 2 present, it covers four slots, and 5 covers at most two of the opposite parity while the third prime covers at most one. With 2 absent, eight hits require 5 covering exactly four and two disjoint admissible pairs. I enumerated a mod 5 independently: the five masks are {2,3,7}, {1,2,6,7}, {0,1,5,6}, {0,4,5}, {3,4}. In the complements of the two size-four masks the only admissible edges share vertex 0 or vertex 7, respectively; no matching. For sharpness, a≡7 mod 10 covers offsets 0,2,4,6 by 2 and 1,5 by 5; CRT with a+3 congruent to a root of −1 mod r covers the final offset for every specified r, with a nonnegative representative. The a=7 example has the missing value 101. The proof covers all prime powers and is not mediated by a finite prime cutoff. VERIFICATION.md and verify.py were read, not executed.

value.rationale: This is the first kind of nontrivial covering obstruction one needs when studying a fixed quadratic with a small prime support: parity and possible pair distances rule out simultaneous coverage even though counting individual hit capacities can allow eight. The exact upper bound settles the entire three-prime class, including arbitrarily large primes and prime powers, with an infinite supply of extremizers. It is not a numerical check on one modulus.
